blocks.text: No government has enough soldiers to stand behind every citizen. Nigeria has more than two hundred million people and a few hundred thousand security personnel. Governments survive because most people obey without being watched — and the name for that willing obedience is legitimacy.

blocks.markdown:
**Legitimacy** is the quality of rightfulness that makes a government's commands acceptable to the governed. A legitimate government is one the people believe *ought* to be obeyed, quite apart from what it can do to them if they refuse.

Legitimacy is therefore a matter of belief, not of force. A regime may control the army, the treasury and the airwaves and still lack legitimacy — and such a regime must spend heavily on coercion to stay in place.

blocks.title: Legitimacy
blocks.text: The general acceptance by the people that a government's acquisition and exercise of power is rightful and in accordance with recognised rules and values.

blocks.markdown:
### Where legitimacy comes from

A government can ground its claim to be rightful in several ways, and strong governments usually rely on more than one.

items: **Constitutionality** — power was acquired and is exercised according to the constitution and the law.
**Free and fair elections** — the rulers were chosen by the people in a credible contest.
**Tradition and heredity** — the office has been filled the same way for generations, as with Nigeria's traditional stools.
**Performance** — the government delivers security, roads, schools, jobs and stable prices, so people accept it because it works.
**Popular consent shown in a referendum or plebiscite** — the people expressly approve the arrangement.
**International recognition** — other states and organisations deal with the government as the lawful authority.

blocks.caption: How to recognise legitimacy in practice

blocks.markdown:
### Political culture and political socialisation

**Political culture** is the pattern of beliefs, attitudes and values a people hold about politics and government — how far citizens trust the state, whether they think voting matters, how they view opposition. Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba distinguished three orientations: the **parochial** culture, where citizens are barely aware of national government; the **subject** culture, where they are aware of it but see themselves only as recipients of its decisions; and the **participant** culture, where they see themselves as entitled to shape those decisions.

**Political socialisation** is the lifelong process by which people acquire that culture. Its main agents are the family, the school, the peer group, religious bodies, the mass media, political parties and trade unions. A citizen who grows up watching every election disputed learns a different politics from one who grows up watching losers concede.

blocks.title: Assessing the legitimacy of a regime
blocks.prompt: A military government seizes power, suspends the constitution, rules by decree, and after two years announces free elections which it conducts credibly and then hands over. Assess its legitimacy at each stage.

steps.text: Stage one — the seizure. Power was taken outside the constitution, so the regime begins with no constitutional legitimacy and no electoral mandate.

Stage two — early rule. If it restores order and delivers services, it may acquire limited performance legitimacy, sometimes strengthened by international recognition. This is legitimacy by results, and it is fragile.

Stage three — the transition. Conducting a credible election restores the electoral and constitutional bases of legitimacy, but for the successor government, not retrospectively for the military regime itself.
Conclusion: legitimacy is not all-or-nothing. Judge it separately against each source — constitutional, electoral, performance and traditional — and say which are satisfied.

blocks.answer: Initially illegitimate in constitutional and electoral terms, possibly gaining limited performance legitimacy, and finally transferring restored legitimacy to an elected successor rather than earning it itself

blocks.title: Do not confuse legality with legitimacy
blocks.text: An act can be legal but illegitimate — for example a law passed by a proper procedure that the people regard as unjust. It can also be legitimate but of doubtful legality, as when a widely supported traditional practice has no statutory backing. Say clearly that legality tests conformity to rules while legitimacy tests popular acceptance.

points: Legitimacy is popular acceptance that a government's power is rightful.
Its main sources are constitutionality, credible elections, tradition, performance, popular consent and international recognition.
Where legitimacy is high, obedience is voluntary and the cost of coercion falls.
Political culture is a people's pattern of political beliefs; Almond and Verba classified it as parochial, subject or participant.
Political socialisation transmits political culture through family, school, peer group, religion, media and parties.
